questions.q: Per this lesson's five-question design process, how should the 'fact' behind a new event be stated?
options: As an instruction telling a subscriber what to do
As a past-tense sentence describing something that already happened
As a SOQL query
As a list of every possible subscriber's desired reaction
questions.explain: Question 1 of the process asks for the fact stated as a past-tense sentence — a command disguised as a notification violates the 'fact, not command' rule from Lesson 9.

questions.q: In the worked support-case example, why isn't `Case_Critical_Escalation__e` simply the raw CDC change event on Case?
options: Because CDC cannot be enabled on standard objects like Case
Because the escalation fact depends on two conditions together (Priority and case age), which is a derived, calculated moment rather than a single raw field change
Because custom platform events are always faster than CDC events
Because Case does not support platform event triggers
questions.explain: The escalation fact is derived from a multi-condition check (priority AND age), so it's calculated by Apex reacting to the CDC change, which then publishes a purpose-built custom event — not something CDC's raw field-change event alone expresses.

questions.q: In the worked example, which subscriber's reaction was idempotent on its own, needing no EventUuid tracking?
options: The external Slack-style Tier 2 notification
The dashboard counter increment
The Account CSAT-risk flag-set (CSAT_Risk__c = true)
All three subscribers needed tracking
questions.explain: Setting CSAT_Risk__c = true produces the same end result whether it runs once or multiple times, so it's naturally idempotent — unlike a notification send or a counter increment, which both duplicate their effect on repeated delivery.

questions.q: What does question 3 of the five-question process ('who are the realistic subscribers, and what does each one need to act?') directly drive?
options: Whether to use Apex or Flow to publish the event
The thin-event/fat-event decision from Lesson 9 — designing payload fields for the subscribers you can actually name
Whether the event should be high-volume or standard-volume
Whether CDC should be enabled at all
questions.explain: Naming the realistic subscribers and what each needs is exactly the input to the thin-event/fat-event trade-off — designing for named subscribers rather than guessing at hypothetical future ones.

questions.q: What does question 5 of the five-question process ask you to check for?
options: Whether the event is published from Flow or Apex
Whether any subscriber depends on this event's timing relative to another event, which would require an explicit sequence/timestamp field rather than relying on arrival order
Whether the subscriber uses lightning/empApi or Pub/Sub API
Whether the event definition includes a picklist field
questions.explain: Question 5 checks for cross-event ordering dependencies, which — per Lesson 6 and Lesson 10 — need an explicit sequence or timestamp field in the schema rather than trusting delivery order alone.
